Define the potential difference across a component as the energy transferred per unit charge. The word per states a ratio, V equals W over Q. Energy is in joules, charge in coulombs, so one volt equals one joule per coulomb. A potential difference of five volts means five joules is transferred for each coulomb through that component.
Charge is the quantity moved through the component, the energy transfer depends on both that charge and the potential difference across it.

Recall and use P equals V I for electrical power. From P equals W over t, W equals V Q and I equals Q over t, it follows that P equals V I. nine point two Potential difference and power.
In one breath.
Potential difference tells you how much energy is transferred for each coulomb passing through a component. Power tells you how quickly that transfer happens.
Key ideas.

Potential difference across a component is the energy transferred per unit charge. If energy W is transferred when charge Q passes through the component, then. V equals W over Q. The unit is the volt, one volt equals one joule per coulomb. For instance, six point zero volts means six point zero joules is transferred for each coulomb passing through the component. Write per unit charge in a definition, merely saying energy transferred by a unit charge does not clearly state the ratio.

Rearrange the same equation to find energy or charge, W equals V Q and Q equals W over V. Keep joules, coulombs and volts consistent. A charge of four point zero coulombs through a component at three point zero volts transfers twelve joules.

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, P equals W over t. Since current is charge per second, I equals Q over t, replacing W by V Q gives. P equals V Q over t equals V I. This works for a component when V is the potential difference across that component and I is its current. The unit of power is the watt, one watt equals one joule per second. If V or I varies with time, V I gives the power at that instant.

For a resistor with V equals I R, substitution gives two further useful forms, P equals I squared R, and, P equals V squared over R. Choose the version matching the quantities you know. The same resistor has the same R when comparing two operating points, so P is proportional to I squared and P is proportional to V squared. A current multiplied by one point five therefore makes the power one point five squared equals two point two five times as great. Conversely, a power increase of fifty percent makes the current the square root of one point five times as great, provided the resistance stays fixed.

Measuring potential difference, To measure the potential difference across a lamp, connect a voltmeter in parallel with that lamp, one terminal at each side. Its terminals compare the potentials of those two connection points, so the reading refers to energy transferred per unit charge across the named lamp.

Method.
Identify the component and the energy, charge, potential difference, current, resistance or time that belongs to it. Do not silently use the supply voltage for a different component.

For energy per charge, start with V equals W over Q and rearrange if needed. For power, use P equals V I, if the component obeys V equals I R, choose I squared R or V squared over R when those avoid an extra step.

Convert units first, for example, forty milliamperes equals zero point zero four zero amperes and one point zero hours equals three thousand six hundred seconds. Substitute with units, calculate, then check sensible significant figures.
Worked example.

A fixed zero point eight zero ohms resistor dissipates seven point two watts. Its power rises by fifty percent. Calculate the new current. The new power is one point five times seven point two equals ten point eight watts. Use P equals I squared R because resistance is fixed. I equals the square root of P over R, end root, equals the square root of ten point eight over zero point eight zero, end root, equals three point seven amperes. The current rises by about twenty two percent, not fifty percent, because power depends on its square.
Traps.
Trap, Calling potential difference energy transferred by a unit charge. Why it's wrong, This can sound like an energy, whereas voltage is a ratio. Instead, Say energy transferred per unit charge.
Trap, Dividing energy by current to find voltage. Why it's wrong, Current is charge per second. Instead, Use V equals W over Q, with charge in coulombs.
Trap, Treating power as proportional to current for a fixed resistor. Why it's wrong, P equals I squared R. Instead, Square the current ratio, or square root the power ratio.

Trap, Using P equals V squared over R to compare series resistors as though they had the same voltage. Why it's wrong, Series components share current, while their p. d. s can differ. Instead, Use the common current and P equals I squared R.
Exam technique.

For Define, give the precise ratio in words. For Calculate or Determine, state the equation before substituting values and show the unit. For Show that, display the algebra and substitution so the stated result follows clearly. In a circuit question, label which voltage and current belong to the named component, this prevents applying a supply value to the wrong resistor.
